blocks.text: And on the dust they are warmed] In Hebrew תחמם, is warmed; supply each one of the eggs. This is an enallage of number, of which we spoke just now. Others render warms, which does not fit with what precedes [II, 858]: She leaves her eggs, and warms them. For the ostrich does not warm the very eggs it has left. To avoid this difficulty Saint Jerome changed the person thus: When she abandons her eggs on the ground, will you perhaps warm them in the dust? For the verb תחמם can be second person masculine as well as third person feminine. But he added you perhaps of his own, and omitted the conjunction AND, which does not allow this change of person. For it is not correct to say, When she leaves her eggs on the ground, and you will warm them in the dust, for will you warm them in the dust? I have therefore preferred to render and on the dust it is warmed, although תחמם is in Piel, a conjugation which very often has an active meaning, but sometimes also an intransitive one. Further, the eggs, deserted by the mother, are said to be warmed, not with the heat that gives life, but with the heat that corrupts. For the interpreters' view that they are hatched by the heat of the sun alone, or by the warmth of the dust alone, without the mother's help, is a mere dream, which the commentators draw from Isidore, Albertus, Cardano, Vallés, etc. But the Arabs teach that these deserted eggs are corrupted and rot, as will be noted below. Yet, if we believe Damiri, ومن اعاجيب النعامة انها تضع بيضها طولا بحيث لو مد عليه خيط لم يجد لشي منه خروجا عن الاخر ثم تعطي كل بيضة نصيبها من الحضن ان كان كل بدنها لا يشتمل علي عدد بيضها [wa-min aʿājīb al-naʿāma annahā taḍaʿu bayḍahā ṭūlan bi-ḥaythu law mudda ʿalayhi khayṭ lam yajid li-shay minhu khurūjan ʿan al-ākhar thumma tuʿṭī kull bayḍa naṣībahā min al-ḥaḍn in kāna kull badanihā lā yashtamil ʿalī ʿadad bayḍihā] Among the marvels of the ostrich is also this, that it arranges its eggs lengthwise in such a way that, if a thread were stretched over them, not a single one would be found to project beyond another. When this is done, each egg receives its share of her incubation, although her body cannot cover them all. This happens, as they would have it, through the transmission of a power, as in a chain of iron rings, if one is rubbed on a magnet, the rest follow the first.

And she forgets that a foot may crush them] The Greeks have σκορπιεῖ [skorpiei], and the Chaldee תבדרנה, may scatter them; but the Hebrew תזורה is from the verb זור, to crush, not from זרה, to scatter. The Syriac, with no sense at all, has ܘܛܥܝܐ ܕܪܓܠܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ̇, And she forgets that she has the foot of a bird: as if for רגל תזורה he had read רגל צפור לה; which is quite beside the point, and indeed false. For the ostrich does not have a toed foot like birds, but a cloven one like quadrupeds. The Philosopher, On the Parts of Animals, book 4, chapter 14: Δίπους μέν ἐστιν, ὡς ὄρνις· διχηλὸς δὲ ὡς τετράπους· οὐ γὰρ δακτύλους ἔχει, ἀλλὰ χηλάς [Dipous men estin, hōs ornis; dichēlos de hōs tetrapous; ou gar daktylous echei, alla chēlas]. It is two-footed, like a bird, but cloven-hoofed, like a quadruped; for it does not have toes, but a cloven hoof. So it truly does not have the foot of a bird. But the Hebrew is plain [col. 254]: She forgets that a foot may crush them; that is, she is so stupid that she does not consider [II, 859] that it may happen that her eggs, which she has left on the ground, are trodden by the feet of wild beasts or of men. As if it made no difference to her whether they are crushed or not. As if Ulysses had not turned aside his plough when, as he was ploughing, his son was laid in the furrow he was drawing.
